name: CJC-1295 with DAC
summary: A long-acting, lab-made version of the hormone that triggers growth hormone release, taken to raise growth hormone and IGF-1; human data come from short studies in healthy adults.
what_it_is: CJC-1295 with DAC is a synthetic, 29-amino-acid analog of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH), the brain signal that tells the pituitary gland to release growth hormone. It carries an extra chemical unit at one end (MPA-lysine, the 'DAC'), part of a design meant to latch onto albumin, a blood protein, so its half-life stretches to about 6 to 8 days instead of minutes. It reached early human studies but is not an approved medicine.

evidence.why: Two small 2006 studies in healthy adults showed higher growth hormone and IGF-1 for days after injection; FDA found no data on effectiveness for any health outcome.

status_us.label: Not approved; FDA advisers voted against compounding
status_us.note: In December 2024 FDA's compounding advisory committee voted 13-0 against adding CJC-1295 DAC to the list of substances pharmacies may compound. FDA has moved it off its Category 2 'significant safety risks' list only because the nomination was withdrawn, and it is not in Category 1, so there is no clear legal compounding route; WADA bans it in sport.

benefits.claim: Raised growth hormone and IGF-1 above baseline for days after a single injection in healthy adults
Raised baseline growth hormone between pulses (not peak levels) and lifted IGF-1 about 40% a week after one dose in healthy adults

risks.risk: Side effects in 94% of volunteers after one injection in the first human study, mostly injection-site reactions (about 70%)
Flushing and body-wide vasodilatory reactions, headache, nausea, dizziness and low blood pressure after repeat injections; increased heart rate in a second study
One death from a heart attack was reported in a halted, unpublished HIV trial; the treating physician blamed existing heart disease, and causality was not established
Animal studies found lower hemoglobin, higher cholesterol, injection-site tissue damage and DNA damage in pituitary cells; no cancer studies exist
Possible immune reactions from impurities; FDA judged all CJC-1295 forms 'not well characterized' for compounding

Long-term safety unknown; FDA says the known risks of raised growth hormone and IGF-1 should be assumed, such as the fluid retention and higher blood sugar on the label of tesamorelin, which works the same way

avoid_if: Active cancer or a history of pituitary tumors
Heart disease or heart rhythm problems
Pregnant or breastfeeding (no full reproductive studies)
Competitive athletes (prohibited by WADA at all times)

before: General health check with a clinician
during: IGF-1 (one dose group in a study rose above the normal range)
labs.why: No evidence-based monitoring exists for CJC-1295; FDA says growth hormone and IGF-1 risks should be assumed, and the label of tesamorelin (same mechanism) monitors IGF-1 and blood sugar.

studies.title: Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee meeting transcript, December 4, 2024 (morning session: CJC-1295)
studies.people: FDA review of two small studies in healthy adults (one with 12 men) plus rat and dog studies
studies.finding: Growth hormone and IGF-1 rose for days after injection and side effects were frequent, mostly injection-site and vasodilatory reactions. FDA found no information on effectiveness for growth hormone deficiency.

studies.title: Growth Hormone Doping in Sports: A Critical Review of Use and Detection Strategies
studies.people: Review of published research, including CJC-1295 studies in healthy adults
studies.finding: Reports a half-life of 6 to 8 days, higher baseline growth hormone and about 40% higher IGF-1 a week after one dose; calls the effect moderate and notes long-acting GHRH analogs have reached the black market.

ask_your_clinician: Is there a lawful, quality-checked source for this, or is an approved option better for my goal?
Given my heart health, blood pressure and blood sugar, is a long-acting growth hormone booster safe for me?
If I compete in a tested sport, would this cause an anti-doping violation?

notes_for_editor: The primary papers (Teichman 2006; Ionescu and Frohman 2006, J Clin Endocrinol Metab) were not opened because the web-search budget ran out; their findings are taken from FDA's December 2024 PCAC presentation (source 5) and the 2012 Endocrine Reviews summary. The death report is described by FDA as anecdotal (found by internet search, unpublished trial). The transcript title is descriptive (FDA posts it as a download). Seed correction: CJC-1295 is not 'awaiting formal committee review' - the committee already voted against all five CJC-1295 forms in December 2024, and it is not on the 2026-27 PCAC agendas. The FDA Law Blog (source 8) mentions a lawsuit over CJC-1295, ipamorelin, AOD-9604 and thymosin alpha-1 with no outcome reported, so status could change; 'no clear legal compounding route' is an inference from FDA's 503A rules.
